claim: The brain has a remarkable capacity to acquire and store memories that can later be selectively recalled.
source: The brain has a remarkable capacity to acquire and store memories that can later be selectively recalled.
evidence: This is a general statement about brain function that draws from established scientific consensus.

claim: Memory processes are supported by the hippocampus.
source: These processes are supported by the hippocampus which is thought to index memory recall by reinstating information stored across distributed neocortical circuits.
evidence: This statement draws from established scientific knowledge about hippocampal function.

claim: The hippocampus indexes memory recall by reinstating information stored across distributed neocortical circuits.
source: These processes are supported by the hippocampus which is thought to index memory recall by reinstating information stored across distributed neocortical circuits.
evidence: This is a theoretical framework cited from existing literature.

claim: Recall of a visual cue from a paired associate is accompanied by a transient increase in the ratio between glutamate and GABA in visual cortex.
source: Here, in humans, we show that recall of a visual cue from a paired associate is accompanied by a transient increase in the ratio between glutamate and GABA in visual cortex.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript (Figure 4).

claim: Excitatory-inhibitory fluctuations in visual cortex are predicted by activity in the hippocampus.
source: Moreover, these excitatory-inhibitory fluctuations are predicted by activity in the hippocampus.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript (Figure 5).

claim: The hippocampus gates memory recall by indexing information stored across neocortical circuits using a disinhibitory mechanism.
source: These data suggest the hippocampus gates memory recall by indexing information stored across neocortical circuits using a disinhibitory mechanism.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings, involving inference from the data.

claim: Memories are thought to be stored across sparse and distributed neuronal ensembles in the brain.
source: Memories are thought to be stored across sparse and distributed neuronal ensembles in the brain (Buzsáki, 2010; Josselyn and Tonegawa, 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to other scholarly work.

claim: During memory recall, activity across neuronal ensembles is selectively reinstated to recover enduring representations of the past.
source: During memory recall, activity across these neuronal ensembles is selectively reinstated to recover enduring representations of the past.
evidence: This is based on established scientific knowledge about memory processes.

claim: Memory reinstatement is thought to be mediated by the hippocampus.
source: This reinstatement is thought to be mediated by the hippocampus, a brain region important for learning and memory (Squire, 1992).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to scholarly work.

claim: The hippocampus sits at the apex of a cortical sensory processing hierarchy.
source: Anatomically, the hippocampus sits at the apex of a cortical sensory processing hierarchy (Felleman and Essen, 1991) where inputs received by sensory cortices reach the hippocampus via the entorhinal cortex and other relay regions, which in turn make widespread cortico-cortical connections that project the hippocampal output back to neocortex (Witter, 1993; Witter et al., 1989).
evidence: This anatomical description is supported by citations to other scholarly work.

claim: Inputs from sensory cortices reach the hippocampus via the entorhinal cortex and other relay regions.
source: Anatomically, the hippocampus sits at the apex of a cortical sensory processing hierarchy (Felleman and Essen, 1991) where inputs received by sensory cortices reach the hippocampus via the entorhinal cortex and other relay regions, which in turn make widespread cortico-cortical connections that project the hippocampal output back to neocortex (Witter, 1993; Witter et al., 1989).
evidence: This anatomical description is supported by citations to other scholarly work.

claim: The entorhinal cortex and relay regions make widespread cortico-cortical connections that project hippocampal output back to neocortex.
source: Anatomically, the hippocampus sits at the apex of a cortical sensory processing hierarchy (Felleman and Essen, 1991) where inputs received by sensory cortices reach the hippocampus via the entorhinal cortex and other relay regions, which in turn make widespread cortico-cortical connections that project the hippocampal output back to neocortex (Witter, 1993; Witter et al., 1989).
evidence: This anatomical description is supported by citations to other scholarly work.

claim: Reciprocal anatomical connectivity equips the hippocampus with the necessary architecture to coordinate activity in neocortex.
source: This reciprocal anatomical connectivity equips the hippocampus with the necessary architecture to coordinate activity in neocortex.
evidence: This is an inference based on the anatomical connectivity described.

claim: The hippocampus may be considered to provide a 'memory index' for information stored across distributed cortical circuits.
source: The hippocampus may therefore be considered to provide a 'memory index', or summary sketch, for information stored across distributed cortical circuits (Goode et al., 2020; Teyler and DiScenna, 1985; Teyler and Rudy, 2007).
evidence: This theoretical framework is supported by citations to other scholarly work.

claim: During memory recall, hippocampal reinstatement predicts subsequent neocortical reinstatement.
source: Consistent with this view, during memory recall, hippocampal reinstatement predicts subsequent neocortical reinstatement (Pacheco Estefan et al., 2019; Tanaka et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to other scholarly work.

claim: The mechanism that allows the hippocampus to coordinate reinstatement across distributed neocortical circuits remains unclear.
source: However, the mechanism that allows the hippocampus to coordinate reinstatement across distributed neocortical circuits remains unclear.
evidence: This identifies a gap in current knowledge.

claim: The hippocampus may shape computations performed by neocortical circuits by modulating the dynamic interplay between excitation and inhibition.
source: One possibility is that the hippocampus shapes computations performed by neocortical circuits by modulating the dynamic interplay between excitation and inhibition (EI).
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: Tight coupling between neocortical excitation and inhibition can be observed during both sensory stimulation and spontaneous neural activity at the cellular level.
source: At the cellular level, tight coupling between neocortical EI can be observed during both sensory stimulation and spontaneous neural activity (Haider et al., 2006; McCormick et al., 2004; Okun and Lampl, 2008; Wehr and Zador, 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to other scholarly work.

claim: EI balance is maintained to hold memories in a silent and dormant state.
source: Evidence in humans, animal models, and theoretical models together suggests that EI balance is maintained to hold memories in a silent and dormant state (Barron et al., 2016; Froemke et al., 2007; Vallentin et al., 2016; Vogels et al., 2011), thus protecting memories from interference caused by new learning (Koolschijn et al., 2019; Kuchibhotla et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to other scholarly work.

claim: EI balance protects memories from interference caused by new learning.
source: Evidence in humans, animal models, and theoretical models together suggests that EI balance is maintained to hold memories in a silent and dormant state (Barron et al., 2016; Froemke et al., 2007; Vallentin et al., 2016; Vogels et al., 2011), thus protecting memories from interference caused by new learning (Koolschijn et al., 2019; Kuchibhotla et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to other scholarly work.

claim: During recall, EI balance must be transiently disturbed if memories are to be released from inhibitory control.
source: During recall, however, EI balance must be transiently disturbed if memories are to be released from inhibitory control.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the concept of EI balance maintaining dormant memories.

claim: Memory recall involves a transient break in EI balance, opening a window to release memories from inhibition before network stability is re-established.
source: Here, we predict that memory recall involves a transient break in EI balance, opening a window to release memories from the blanket of inhibition before network stability is re-established.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: The transient break in neocortical EI balance is mediated by activity in the hippocampus.
source: Moreover, we predict that this transient break in neocortical EI balance is mediated by activity in the hippocampus.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: A new imaging sequence combining fMRI with fMRS was implemented in humans.
source: To test these predictions, here, we implemented a new imaging sequence in humans that combines functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) with functional magnetic resonance spectroscopy (fMRS) (Ip et al., 2019; Ip et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the study, with citations to previous work.

claim: The combined fMRI-fMRS sequence provides an opportunity to monitor activity in the hippocampus with fMRI while simultaneously measuring time-resolved fluctuations in neocortical glutamate and GABA using fMRS.
source: This sequence provides an opportunity to monitor activity in the hippocampus with fMRI while simultaneously measuring time-resolved fluctuations in neocortical glutamate and GABA using fMRS.
evidence: This describes the capabilities of the methodology used.

claim: MRS provides a unique tool to quantify the concentration of different neural metabolites.
source: MRS provides a unique tool to quantify the concentration of different neural metabolites (De Graaf, 2019; Mangia et al., 2012), including glutamate and GABA, the principle excitatory and inhibitory neurotransmitters in the brain.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to other scholarly work.

claim: MRS can quantify glutamate and GABA, the principle excitatory and inhibitory neurotransmitters in the brain.
source: MRS provides a unique tool to quantify the concentration of different neural metabolites (De Graaf, 2019; Mangia et al., 2012), including glutamate and GABA, the principle excitatory and inhibitory neurotransmitters in the brain.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge.

claim: MRS cannot dissociate between neurotransmitter and metabolic pools of glutamate and GABA.
source: MRS cannot dissociate between neurotransmitter and metabolic pools of glutamate and GABA (Bak et al., 2006; Magistretti and Allaman, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to other scholarly work.

claim: There is an approximately 1:1 relationship between the rate of glutamine-glutamate cycling and neuronal oxidative glucose consumption.
source: However, meaningful interpretation of MRS nevertheless derives from a major body of work showing an approximately 1:1 relationship between the rate of glutamine-glutamate cycling, which is necessary for glutamate and GABA synthesis, and neuronal oxidative glucose consumption, which indirectly supports neurotransmitter release among other processes (Rothman et al., 2003; Shen et al., 1999; Sibson et al., 1998).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to other scholarly work.

claim: MRS can provide a non-invasive marker for physiologically relevant EI at a coarse spatiotemporal scale.
source: Therefore, while measures of EI balance vary in both definition and granularity, MRS can provide a non-invasive marker for physiologically relevant EI at a coarse spatiotemporal scale.
evidence: This is an inference based on the properties of MRS and the relationship between metabolic and neurotransmitter pools.

claim: MRS-derived glutamate and GABA reported during learning and memory paradigms show remarkable consistency with findings reported at the physiological level in animals.
source: Correspondingly, MRS-derived glutamate and GABA reported during learning and memory paradigms show remarkable consistency with findings reported at the physiological level in animals (Barron et al., 2016; Castro-Alamancos et al., 1995; Floyer-Lea et al., 2006; Froemke et al., 2007; Kolasinski et al., 2019; Lunghi et al., 2015; Trepel and Racine, 2000; Vallentin et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to other scholarly work.

claim: During memory recall, there is a transient increase in the ratio between MRS-derived glutamate and GABA in neocortex.
source: Using the combined fMRI-fMRS sequence, here, we implemented a task designed to engage hippocampal-dependent recall of a visual cue. During memory recall, we report a transient increase in the ratio between MRS-derived glutamate and GABA in neocortex which is selectively predicted by the blood oxygen level-dependent (BOLD) signal in the hippocampus.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data.

claim: The transient increase in the ratio between MRS-derived glutamate and GABA in neocortex is selectively predicted by the BOLD signal in the hippocampus.
source: Using the combined fMRI-fMRS sequence, here, we implemented a task designed to engage hippocampal-dependent recall of a visual cue. During memory recall, we report a transient increase in the ratio between MRS-derived glutamate and GABA in neocortex which is selectively predicted by the blood oxygen level-dependent (BOLD) signal in the hippocampus.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data.

claim: The hippocampus coordinates memory recall by transiently perturbing neocortical EI balance to release memories stored across distributed neural circuits.
source: These findings suggest the hippocampus coordinates memory recall by transiently perturbing neocortical EI balance to release memories stored across distributed neural circuits.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: The inference task has previously been shown to involve associative memory recall in humans.
source: This task has previously been shown to involve associative memory recall in humans (Barron et al., 2020; Koster et al., 2018) and mice (Barron et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to other scholarly work.

claim: Associative recall required for inference is a hippocampal-dependent process.
source: Unlike some forms of associative recall, previous lesion and optogenetic studies in rodents demonstrate that associative recall required for inference is a hippocampal-dependent process (Barron et al., 2020; Bunsey and Eichenbaum, 1996; DeVito et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to other scholarly work.

claim: The inference task provides an opportunity to investigate whether activity in the hippocampus mediates dynamic changes in neocortical EI during memory recall.
source: Thus, the inference task provides an opportunity to investigate whether activity in the hippocampus mediates dynamic changes in neocortical EI during memory recall.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the properties of the inference task.

claim: Participants learned up to 80 auditory-visual associations during the associative learning stage.
source: In the first stage of the task, participants learned up to 80 auditory-visual associations ('associative learning', day 1; Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Each visual cue was paired with either a rewarding or neutral outcome during the conditioning stage.
source: In the second stage, which occurred approximately 24 hr later, each visual cue was paired with either a rewarding (set 1, monetary reward) or neutral outcome (set 2, woodchip) delivered to a wooden box in the corner of the VR environment ('conditioning', day 2; Figure 1A–B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Auditory cues were never paired with an outcome during conditioning.
source: Auditory cues were never paired with an outcome, providing an opportunity to assess evidence for an inferred relationship between these indirectly related stimuli.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Participants performed the inference test inside the 7T MRI scanner.
source: Participants performed the inference test during an MRI scan (Figure 1C–D, Figure 1—video 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: Behaviour during the inference test revealed a significant interaction between the response to auditory cues in set 1 and 2 and whether participants indicated they wanted to look in the box.
source: Behaviour during the inference test revealed a significant interaction between the response to auditory cues in set 1 and 2 ("rewarded" and "neutral") and whether or not the participants indicated that they wanted to look in the box ("yes" and "no") (two-way ANOVA, F1,72 = 630.99, p < 0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the behavioral data, shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Participants pressed 'yes' more often for auditory cues in set 1 (rewarded).
source: Tukey's post hoc test showed participants pressed "yes" more often for auditory cues in set 1 (p < 0.001), and "no" more often for auditory cues in set 2 (p < 0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the behavioral data, shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Participants pressed 'no' more often for auditory cues in set 2 (neutral).
source: Tukey's post hoc test showed participants pressed "yes" more often for auditory cues in set 1 (p < 0.001), and "no" more often for auditory cues in set 2 (p < 0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the behavioral data, shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Inferential behaviour was observed despite participants never experiencing the outcomes in response to the auditory cues.
source: This inferential behaviour was observed despite participants never experiencing the outcomes in response to the auditory cues.
evidence: This is an observation about the experimental design and results.

claim: During the post-scan associative test, participants remembered 55% of the auditory-visual associations.
source: During the post-scan associative test, participants remembered 55% of the auditory-visual associations (54.8% ± 1.78%; mean ± SEM), significantly above chance as indicated by the dotted line (t18 = 29.96, p < 0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the behavioral data, shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Participants' memory for auditory-visual associations was significantly above chance.
source: During the post-scan associative test, participants remembered 55% of the auditory-visual associations (54.8% ± 1.78%; mean ± SEM), significantly above chance as indicated by the dotted line (t18 = 29.96, p < 0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the behavioral data, shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Participants successfully inferred the appropriate outcome on trials where they could later recall the correct auditory-visual association.
source: In response to auditory cues during the inference test (Figure 1D), participants successfully inferred the appropriate outcome (Figure 1E) on trials where they could later recall the correct auditory-visual association in the post-scan associative test ('correct association': t18 = 22.91, p < 0.001; 'incorrect association': t18 = 0.09, p = 0.925; 'correct association'–'incorrect association': t18 = 16.21, p < 0.001; dotted line indicates chance).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the behavioral data, shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Behavioural performance on the inference test was predicted by behavioural performance on the post-scan associative test.
source: Across participants, behavioural performance on the inference test was predicted by behavioural performance on the post-scan associative test (r17 = 0.57, p = 0.010).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the behavioral data, shown in Figure 2D.

claim: There was no significant effect of sex on behavioural performance.
source: Notably, there was no significant effect of sex on behavioural performance (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the behavioral data.

claim: BOLD signal in the visual cortex was significantly higher for 'remembered' versus 'forgotten' auditory cues during the question period.
source: During the question period in the inference test (Figure 1C–D), BOLD signal in the visual cortex and the hippocampus was significantly higher for 'remembered' versus 'forgotten' auditory cues ('remembered'–'forgotten', visual cortex: t17 = 5.92, p < 0.001; hippocampus: t17 = 4.33, p = 0.017; whole-volume family wise error (FWE)-corrected; together with regions listed in Supplementary file 4; Montreal Neurological Institute [MNI] coordinates).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the fMRI data, shown in Figure 3C.

claim: BOLD signal in the hippocampus was significantly higher for 'remembered' versus 'forgotten' auditory cues during the question period.
source: During the question period in the inference test (Figure 1C–D), BOLD signal in the visual cortex and the hippocampus was significantly higher for 'remembered' versus 'forgotten' auditory cues ('remembered'–'forgotten', visual cortex: t17 = 5.92, p < 0.001; hippocampus: t17 = 4.33, p = 0.017; whole-volume family wise error (FWE)-corrected; together with regions listed in Supplementary file 4; Montreal Neurological Institute [MNI] coordinates).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the fMRI data, shown in Figure 3C.

claim: During the question period of the inference test, glu/GABA ratio significantly increased during 'remembered' versus 'forgotten' trials.
source: During the question period of the inference test trials (up to 3 s), glu/GABA ratio significantly increased during 'remembered' versus 'forgotten' trials ('remembered':'forgotten', glu/GABA ratio: t17 = 2.21, p = 0.041).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the fMRS data, shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: The break in glu/GABA ratio was not observed during the 'tone' or inter-trial interval periods.
source: This break in glu/GABA ratio was not observed during the 'tone' (~7 s) or inter-trial interval ('ITI') (~2.7 s) periods ('tone', glu/GABA ratio: t18 = 1.01, p = 0.325; 'ITI', glu/GABA ratio: t18 = 0.40, p = 0.692).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the fMRS data, shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: Relative to null distributions, GABA significantly decreased while glu/GABA ratio significantly increased during 'remembered' versus 'forgotten' trials.
source: Relative to the null distributions, GABA significantly decreased while glu/GABA ratio significantly increased (glutamate:tCr: p = 0.089; GABA:tCr: p = 0.014; glu/GABA ratio: p = 0.007).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the fMRS data using permutation testing, shown in Figure 4D-F.

claim: The observed GABA ratio measured in vivo was significant relative to the null distribution from Monte Carlo simulations.
source: Relative to this null distribution, the observed GABA ratio measured in vivo (shown in E) was significant (p = 0.019).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from Monte Carlo simulations, shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The increase in hippocampal BOLD signal during 'remembered' compared to 'forgotten' trials positively predicted the decrease in GABA in V1.
source: Across participants, the increase in hippocampal BOLD signal during 'remembered' compared to 'forgotten' trials positively predicted the decrease in GABA and the increase in glu/GABA ratio observed in primary visual cortex (V1) (Figure 4) (glutamate:tCr [total creatine]: r15 = 0.14, p = 0.585; GABA:tCr: r15 = −0.56, p = 0.022; glu/GABA ratio: r15 = 0.52, p = 0.033).
evidence: This is a statistical finding showing correlation between fMRI and fMRS data, shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The increase in hippocampal BOLD signal during 'remembered' compared to 'forgotten' trials positively predicted the increase in glu/GABA ratio in V1.
source: Across participants, the increase in hippocampal BOLD signal during 'remembered' compared to 'forgotten' trials positively predicted the decrease in GABA and the increase in glu/GABA ratio observed in primary visual cortex (V1) (Figure 4) (glutamate:tCr [total creatine]: r15 = 0.14, p = 0.585; GABA:tCr: r15 = −0.56, p = 0.022; glu/GABA ratio: r15 = 0.52, p = 0.033).
evidence: This is a statistical finding showing correlation between fMRI and fMRS data, shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Across the imaged brain volume, the correlation between the BOLD signal and V1 glu/GABA ratio was selectively observed in the left hippocampus.
source: Across the imaged brain volume, for 'remembered' versus 'forgotten' trials, the correlation between the BOLD signal and V1 glu/GABA ratio was selectively observed in the left hippocampus (t16 = 11.37, p = 0.005, whole-brain family wise error (FWE)-corrected; Supplementary file 7; MNI coordinates).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from whole-brain analysis, shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The hippocampus gates recall of memories stored across distributed neocortical circuits using a disinhibitory mechanism.
source: Accordingly, we propose the hippocampus gates recall of memories stored across distributed neocortical circuits using a disinhibitory mechanism (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, based on the experimental findings.

claim: The neural circuit mechanisms that underlie an increase in glu/GABA ratio during recall may be informed by evidence that the ratio between excitatory and inhibitory synaptic conductances in cortical neurons fluctuate around a stable set point.
source: For example, the neural circuit mechanisms that underlie an increase in glu/GABA ratio during recall may be informed by evidence that the ratio between excitatory and inhibitory synaptic conductances in cortical neurons fluctuate around a stable set point (Anderson et al., 2000; Okun and Lampl, 2008; Wehr and Zador, 2003; Wilent and Contreras, 2005).
evidence: This is an interpretation linking the findings to circuit-level mechanisms, supported by citations.

claim: Overall EI proportionality ensures that neurons and networks are neither hypo- nor hyper-excitable for prolonged periods.
source: This overall EI proportionality ensures that neurons and networks are neither hypo- nor hyper-excitable for prolonged periods, allowing memories to be held in a dormant state (Barron et al., 2016; Froemke et al., 2007; Vallentin et al., 2016; Vogels et al., 2011) that is protected from interference caused by new learning (Koolschijn et al., 2019; Kuchibhotla et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to other scholarly work.

claim: Transient breaks in EI balance appear necessary for new learning and memory expression.
source: However, despite overall proportionality, the exact E/I ratio is highly dynamic and transient breaks in EI balance appear necessary for new learning and memory expression (Letzkus et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to other scholarly work.

claim: The reported fluctuations in MRS-derived glu/GABA ratio during memory recall may reflect dynamic changes in EI balance.
source: Here, the reported fluctuations in MRS-derived glu/GABA ratio during memory recall may therefore reflect, if indirectly, dynamic changes in EI balance.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Glutamatergic projections from higher-order or interconnected brain regions can target disinhibitory cortical circuits to provide selective EI modulation in rodents.
source: Of particular relevance are studies in rodents which show that glutamatergic projections from higher-order or interconnected brain regions can target disinhibitory cortical circuits to provide selective EI modulation (Krabbe et al., 2019; Lee et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to other scholarly work.

claim: Projections from the cingulate region of mouse frontal cortex modulate activity in V1 by targeting VIP+ interneurons during attentional modulation.
source: For example, to enhance visual discrimination during attentional modulation, projections from the cingulate region of mouse frontal cortex modulate activity in V1 by targeting vasoactive intestinal polypeptide-expressing (VIP+) interneurons, which in turn preferentially target other interneuron subtypes to release excitatory principle cells from inhibitory control (Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to other scholarly work.

claim: During memory recall, hippocampal projections may permit memory reinstatement by targeting disinhibitory circuits in neocortex.
source: During memory recall, hippocampal projections may similarly permit memory reinstatement by targeting disinhibitory circuits in neocortex.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on analogy to findings in animal models.

claim: The correlation between hippocampal activity and glu/GABA ratio may reflect a mechanism whereby activity in the hippocampus facilitates cortical disinhibition.
source: The correlation between hippocampal activity and glu/GABA ratio reported here may therefore reflect a mechanism whereby activity in the hippocampus facilitates cortical disinhibition to release otherwise latent cortical associations from inhibitory control.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claim: The findings are consistent with the notion that the hippocampus provides a memory index to flexibly reinstate information in extrahippocampal circuits.
source: This interpretation of the data is consistent with the notion that the hippocampus provides a memory index to flexibly reinstate information in extrahippocampal circuits (Goode et al., 2020; Teyler and DiScenna, 1985; Teyler and Rudy, 2007).
evidence: This statement connects the findings to existing theoretical frameworks, supported by citations.

claim: The findings replicate equivalent analyses conducted on fMRI data acquired using the same task.
source: Moreover, our findings replicate equivalent analyses conducted on fMRI data acquired using the same task (Barron et al., 2020) and are consistent with previous studies in humans showing evidence for coordinated hippocampal-neocortical memory reinstatement (Horner et al., 2015; Pacheco Estefan et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to other scholarly work.

claim: The findings are consistent with previous studies showing evidence for coordinated hippocampal-neocortical memory reinstatement.
source: Moreover, our findings replicate equivalent analyses conducted on fMRI data acquired using the same task (Barron et al., 2020) and are consistent with previous studies in humans showing evidence for coordinated hippocampal-neocortical memory reinstatement (Horner et al., 2015; Pacheco Estefan et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to other scholarly work.

claim: The results corroborate findings showing that hippocampal glutamate and GABA can predict mnemonic control.
source: When combined with the fMRS data, our results also corroborate findings in humans showing that hippocampal glutamate and GABA can predict mnemonic control (Nikolova et al., 2017; Schmitz et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to other scholarly work.

claim: The relationship between MRS-derived measures of glutamate and GABA and physiological measures of EI balance remains complex.
source: Given this interpretation of the data, we emphasise that the relationship between MRS-derived measures of glutamate and GABA and physiological measures of EI balance remains complex.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the limitations in interpreting MRS data.

claim: Rapid changes in synaptic glutamate and GABA that accompany neurotransmitter release occur on a timescale that is not possible to detect using fMRS.
source: Rapid changes in synaptic glutamate and GABA that accompany neurotransmitter release occur on a timescale that is not possible to detect using fMRS.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the fMRS technique.

claim: Only a fraction of MRS-derived neurometabolite concentration reflects neurotransmitter release.
source: Moreover, only a fraction of MRS-derived neurometabolite concentration reflects neurotransmitter release.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the MRS technique.

claim: MRS is considered most sensitive to unconstrained, intracellular metabolic pools that reside at relatively high concentration in the neuronal cytoplasm.
source: Of the different pools of glutamate and GABA (cytoplasmic, vesicular, or extracellular), MRS is considered most sensitive to unconstrained, intracellular metabolic pools that reside at relatively high concentration in the neuronal cytoplasm (Rae, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to other scholarly work.

claim: Changes in extracellular GABA of less than 100-fold are unlikely to be detectable using MRS.
source: Indeed, changes in extracellular GABA of less than 100-fold are unlikely to be detectable using MRS (Myers et al., 2016) and post-mortem studies suggest MRS is not sensitive to intracellular pools that reside in the mitochondria or vesicles (De Graaf and Bovée, 1990; Kauppinen and Williams, 1991).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to other scholarly work.

claim: Post-mortem studies suggest MRS is not sensitive to intracellular pools that reside in the mitochondria or vesicles.
source: Indeed, changes in extracellular GABA of less than 100-fold are unlikely to be detectable using MRS (Myers et al., 2016) and post-mortem studies suggest MRS is not sensitive to intracellular pools that reside in the mitochondria or vesicles (De Graaf and Bovée, 1990; Kauppinen and Williams, 1991).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to other scholarly work.

claim: The release and recycling of glutamate and GABA constitute major metabolic pathways.
source: Interpretation of MRS-derived glutamate and GABA is further complicated by the fact that the release and recycling of glutamate and GABA constitute major metabolic pathways (Bak et al., 2006; Magistretti and Allaman, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to other scholarly work.

claim: The metabolic and neurotransmitter pools are thought to be tightly coupled during anaesthesia, rest and certain stimulation protocols.
source: Yet, the metabolic and neurotransmitter pools are thought to be tightly coupled during anaesthesia, rest and certain stimulation protocols, with a 1:1 relationship reported between the rate of glutamine-glutamate cycling, which is necessary for glutamate and GABA synthesis, and neuronal oxidative glucose consumption, which indirectly supports neurotransmitter release among other processes (Rothman et al., 2003; Shen et al., 1999; Sibson et al., 1998).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to other scholarly work.

claim: During sensory stimulation a transient uncoupling has been observed with a short-lived mismatch between glucose utilization and oxygen consumption.
source: During sensory stimulation a transient uncoupling has been observed with a short-lived mismatch between glucose utilization and oxygen consumption (Fox et al., 1988; Fox and Raichle, 1986), particularly during stimulation protocols that alternate between high intensity and quiescent periods (Gjedde et al., 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to other scholarly work.

claim: Dynamic fluctuations in fMRS-derived glutamate and GABA may reflect transitions to new metabolic steady states.
source: Dynamic fluctuations in fMRS-derived glutamate and GABA reported here may therefore reflect transitions to new metabolic steady states (Stanley and Raz, 2018), which could reflect (if indirectly) relative shifts in EI equilibrium at the physiological level.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings, supported by a citation.

claim: During associative memory recall, the increase in glu/GABA ratio may be interpreted as an increase in synthesis of glutamate relative to degradation, with an opposing effect on GABA.
source: During associative memory recall, the increase in glu/GABA ratio may therefore be interpreted as an increase in synthesis of glutamate relative to degradation, with an opposing effect on GABA.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Previous studies show event-related changes in MRS glutamate.
source: This interpretation is supported by a handful of previous studies showing event-related changes in MRS glutamate (Apšvalka et al., 2015; Gussew et al., 2010; Lally et al., 2014) and GABA (Cleve et al., 2015), together with a growing body of evidence reporting a relationship between MRS-derived measures of neurometabolites and behaviour (Puts et al., 2011; Scholl et al., 2017; Stagg et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to other scholarly work.

claim: Previous studies show event-related changes in MRS GABA.
source: This interpretation is supported by a handful of previous studies showing event-related changes in MRS glutamate (Apšvalka et al., 2015; Gussew et al., 2010; Lally et al., 2014) and GABA (Cleve et al., 2015), together with a growing body of evidence reporting a relationship between MRS-derived measures of neurometabolites and behaviour (Puts et al., 2011; Scholl et al., 2017; Stagg et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to other scholarly work.

claim: There is a growing body of evidence reporting a relationship between MRS-derived measures of neurometabolites and behaviour.
source: This interpretation is supported by a handful of previous studies showing event-related changes in MRS glutamate (Apšvalka et al., 2015; Gussew et al., 2010; Lally et al., 2014) and GABA (Cleve et al., 2015), together with a growing body of evidence reporting a relationship between MRS-derived measures of neurometabolites and behaviour (Puts et al., 2011; Scholl et al., 2017; Stagg et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to other scholarly work.

claim: It remains to be established whether unconstrained glutamatergic and GABAergic pools show event-related changes that are MRS-sensitive.
source: Nevertheless, it remains to be established whether unconstrained glutamatergic and GABAergic pools show event-related changes that are MRS-sensitive.
evidence: This identifies a limitation and area for future research.

claim: By implementing an inference task in VR, memory recall was operationalized using the exact same paradigm previously employed in rodents.
source: Here, by implementing an inference task in VR, we operationalize memory recall using the exact same paradigm previously employed in rodents (Barron et al., 2020).
evidence: This describes the experimental design, with a citation to previous work.

claim: The findings may be compared to data acquired in animal models in ongoing future research.
source: Therefore, in addition to engaging memory-dependent inference, 'opening the box' to find a reward in the VR environment approximated the process of rodents finding a reward from a dispenser in a 3D environment. By using VR, the findings presented here may be compared to data acquired in animal models in ongoing future research.
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions.

claim: VR paradigms in humans may provide a basis to gain insight into the cellular and circuit mechanisms that underlie macroscopic measures of EI.
source: In this manner, VR paradigms in humans may provide a basis from which to gain insight into the cellular and circuit mechanisms that underlie macroscopic measures of EI.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential utility of the approach.

claim: Previous MRS protocols typically employ a 'block' design where a static measure of glutamate and GABA concentration is achieved by averaging spectra across several minutes.
source: Previous MRS protocols typically employ a 'block' design, where a static measure of the concentration of glutamate and GABA is achieved by averaging the spectra across a time window that may span several minutes.
evidence: This describes typical MRS methodology.

claim: Block design MRS approaches obscure the temporal dynamics of neurometabolites.
source: This approach obscures the temporal dynamics of neurometabolites which more closely relate to fluctuations in EI reported at the physiological level.
evidence: This is a critique of traditional MRS methodology.

claim: When the average concentration of Glx and GABA are considered in V1 across time, no significant relationship is observed across subjects.
source: Indeed, when the average concentration of Glx and GABA are considered in V1 across time, no significant relationship is observed across subjects (Rideaux, 2021), a result which we also observed when assessing average glutamate and GABA using our dataset.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation and confirmed by the authors' own data.

claim: fMRS has emerged as a viable method to detect dynamic changes in neurochemicals in both healthy and clinical populations.
source: By contrast, with the increase in availability of ultra-high field MRI scanners and the development of more advanced sequences (Stagg and Rothman, 2013), fMRS has emerged as a viable method to detect dynamic changes in neurochemicals in both healthy and clinical populations (Stanley and Raz, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to other scholarly work.

claim: fMRS is highly sensitive to detecting task-relevant dynamic changes in glutamate and GABA.
source: Although there are currently only a handful of event-related fMRS studies, together with our data, these suggest that fMRS is highly sensitive to detecting task-relevant dynamic changes in glutamate and GABA (Jelen et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation and the authors' own data.

claim: In the lateral occipital complex, fMRS demonstrates differences in glutamate in response to presentation of objects versus abstract stimuli.
source: For example, in the lateral occipital complex, fMRS demonstrates differences in glutamate in response to presentation of objects versus abstract stimuli (Lally et al., 2014), and in the left anterior insula fMRS reveals a transient increase in glutamate with exposure to painful stimuli (Gussew et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to other scholarly work.

claim: In the left anterior insula, fMRS reveals a transient increase in glutamate with exposure to painful stimuli.
source: For example, in the lateral occipital complex, fMRS demonstrates differences in glutamate in response to presentation of objects versus abstract stimuli (Lally et al., 2014), and in the left anterior insula fMRS reveals a transient increase in glutamate with exposure to painful stimuli (Gussew et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to other scholarly work.

claim: fMRS-derived glutamate is sufficiently sensitive to detect repetition suppression effects in the lateral occipital complex.
source: fMRS-derived glutamate is even sufficiently sensitive to detect repetition suppression effects in the lateral occipital complex (Apšvalka et al., 2015), mirroring analogous effects reported in fMRI (Barron et al., 2016; Grill-Spector et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to other scholarly work.

claim: Within a 3 s time window during the question period, the temporal resolution of fMRS is sufficient to relate transient changes in glutamate and GABA to associative memory recall.
source: Here, we further illustrate that within a 3 s time window delineated by the question period in the inference task, the temporal resolution of fMRS is sufficient to relate transient changes in glutamate and GABA to associative memory recall.
evidence: This is a finding from the current study.

claim: Time-resolved, within-subject, and condition-dependent fMRS may provide a promising tool to capture real-time, task-relevant changes in neurometabolites.
source: Such time-resolved, within-subject, and condition-dependent fMRS may provide a promising tool to capture real-time, task-relevant changes in neurometabolites, on a timescale equivalent to task-based fMRI.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential utility of the approach.

claim: The transient increase in glu/GABA ratio can be accounted for by a significant decrease in the concentration of MRS-derived GABA.
source: During associative memory recall, the transient increase in glu/GABA ratio reported in our data can be accounted for by a significant decrease in the concentration of MRS-derived GABA.
evidence: This is a finding from the current study.

claim: Detecting dynamic changes in GABA is challenging because the concentration of GABA in human brain tissue is relatively low.
source: Notably, detecting dynamic changes in GABA is challenging for two key reasons: the concentration of GABA in human brain tissue is relatively low and the spectral peaks for GABA overlap with other, more abundant neurochemicals (Andreychenko et al., 2012; Govindaraju et al., 2000; Puts and Edden, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to other scholarly work.

claim: Detecting dynamic changes in GABA is challenging because the spectral peaks for GABA overlap with other, more abundant neurochemicals.
source: Notably, detecting dynamic changes in GABA is challenging for two key reasons: the concentration of GABA in human brain tissue is relatively low and the spectral peaks for GABA overlap with other, more abundant neurochemicals (Andreychenko et al., 2012; Govindaraju et al., 2000; Puts and Edden, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to other scholarly work.

claim: The most common approach to detecting MRS-derived GABA involves using a J-difference spectral editing technique.
source: While the most common approach to detecting MRS-derived GABA involves using a J-difference spectral editing technique to separate GABA peaks from overlapping peaks (Bottomley, 1987; Mescher et al., 1998), here we use a non-edited sequence (sLASER).
evidence: This describes typical MRS methodology, supported by citations.

claim: A non-edited MRS sequence was used in this study (sLASER).
source: While the most common approach to detecting MRS-derived GABA involves using a J-difference spectral editing technique to separate GABA peaks from overlapping peaks (Bottomley, 1987; Mescher et al., 1998), here we use a non-edited sequence (sLASER).
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: Spectral editing may provide higher precision but occurs at the cost of a larger volume of interest, longer TEs and higher susceptibility to motion and drift artefacts.
source: While spectral editing may provide higher precision (Hong et al., 2019), this occurs at the cost of a larger volume of interest, longer TEs and higher susceptibility to motion and drift artefacts due to longer acquisition times, making it less suitable for event-related fMRS (Terpstra et al., 2006; Trabesinger and Boesiger, 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to other scholarly work.

claim: Direct comparisons between edited and non-edited sequences at 7 T reveal no significant difference in the concentration of GABA measurements.
source: Moreover, direct comparisons between edited and non-edited sequences at 7 T reveal no significant difference in the concentration of GABA measurements (Hong et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to other scholarly work.

claim: A non-edited sequence can provide sufficient data quality for measuring dynamic changes in MRS-derived GABA.
source: Therefore, together with studies reporting dynamic changes in GABA with sensory stimulation (Lin et al., 2012; Mekle et al., 2017), our data illustrates how a non-edited sequence can provide sufficient data quality for measuring dynamic changes in MRS-derived GABA, which cannot be explained by changes in compounds at higher concentration that have overlapping peaks (i.e. glutamate or NAA, Figure 4—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study, supported by citations to other work.

claim: Monte Carlo simulations validate that non-edited sequences can be used to quantify dynamic changes in GABA.
source: Indeed, Monte Carlo simulations reported here validate that non-edited sequences can be used to quantify dynamic changes in GABA (Figure 4G; Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study using simulations.

claim: The non-edited approach comes with the advantage of simultaneously measuring dynamic changes in GABA and glutamate, together with 17 other neurometabolites.
source: Moreover, compared to spectral editing, our approach comes with the advantage of simultaneously measuring dynamic changes in GABA and glutamate, together with 17 other neurometabolites.
evidence: This describes an advantage of the methodology used.

claim: To detect dynamic changes in GABA, it was necessary to disable default priors on the spectral fitting procedure that constrain GABA as a ratio to more stable metabolite concentrations.
source: To detect dynamic changes in GABA, it was necessary to disable default priors on the spectral fitting procedure that constrain GABA as a ratio to more stable metabolite concentrations (Figure 4—figure supplement 2, see Appendix 1—supplementary note 1).
evidence: This describes a methodological choice made in the study.

claim: Absolute GABA estimates were higher compared to those obtained using default priors that normalise estimates relative to more stable metabolite concentrations.
source: However, we note that absolute GABA estimates were higher compared to those obtained using default priors that normalise estimates relative to more stable metabolite concentrations.
evidence: This is an observation about the methodological approach.

claim: The quality of the MRS data was comparable with other studies that have acquired 7 T MRS data from visual cortex.
source: Importantly, the quality of our MRS data was comparable with other studies that have acquired 7 T MRS data from visual cortex (Bednařík et al., 2018; Hong et al., 2019; Mekle et al., 2017; Prinsen et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to other scholarly work.

claim: The quality of the glutamate estimates was in line with previous studies employing event-related fMRS to assess dynamic changes in glutamate.
source: Moreover, the quality of the glutamate estimates was in line with previous studies employing event-related fMRS to assess dynamic changes in glutamate (Apšvalka et al., 2015; Gussew et al., 2010; Lally et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to other scholarly work.

claim: Disturbances in EI balance are thought to underlie a number of neuropsychiatric conditions.
source: Disturbances in EI balance are thought to underlie a number of neuropsychiatric conditions, including schizophrenia, autism, epilepsy, and Tourette's syndrome (Robertson et al., 2016; Stanley and Raz, 2018; Taylor et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to other scholarly work.

claim: Previous studies report inconsistencies in MRS-derived measures of glutamate and GABA in patient populations.
source: While previous studies report inconsistencies in MRS-derived measures of glutamate and GABA in these patient populations, this may be attributed to differences in brain region, cognitive state, and imaging protocol, among other factors.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature.

claim: The findings present a potential target for clinical investigation.
source: Here, by using both fMRS and fMRI to reveal a signature change in glu/GABA ratio that relates to hippocampal BOLD signal, behavioural performance, and cognition, our findings present a potential target for clinical investigation.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential implications of the findings.

claim: Even in the healthy brain a transient break in EI balance is necessary to support key cognitive processes such as memory recall.
source: Moreover, our findings show that even in the healthy brain a transient break in EI balance is necessary to support key cognitive processes such as memory recall.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings.

claim: Twenty-two healthy human volunteers were included in the study.
source: Twenty-two healthy human volunteers were included in the study (mean age of 22.8 ± 0.74 years, four males).
evidence: This describes the study participants.

claim: All experiments were approved by the University of Oxford ethics committee.
source: All experiments were approved by the University of Oxford ethics committee (reference number R43594/RE001).
evidence: This describes ethical approval for the study.

claim: One participant was excluded from the fMRI and fMRS analyses due to technical difficulties which resulted in the auditory cues not being fully audible during the inference test.
source: Two participants were excluded from the fMRI and fMRS analyses due to technical difficulties which resulted in the auditory cues not being fully audible during the inference test.
evidence: This describes data exclusion criteria.

claim: There was no significant effect of sex on either behavioural performance or MRS measures of glu/GABA ratio during the inference test.
source: Notably, there was no significant effect of sex on either behavioural performance or MRS measures of glu/GABA ratio during the inference test (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study.
